lessons.title: Review — all eight
lessons.gloss: review — the direct object pronouns, complete, and the two questions that pick any one of them

segments.text: Nothing new here. Before the grid: where does an object pronoun sit, and has that ever changed?
Never, in nine chapters. Here is the complete set:

utterances: it / them — masculine. singular: lo. plural: los.
it / them — feminine. singular: la. plural: las.

segments.text: Eight cells, built one at a time, and this is the first page on which they have all appeared together. That is deliberate. A grid handed to you on the day you met the first one would have been eight things to memorise; here it is a picture of ground you already hold.

Count the genuinely new shapes you had to learn across those chapters: me was already yours from chapter four, te was one, nos one, os one, lo one, la one — and los and las were free, because you produced them yourself from an -s.
Reading the grid as eight decisions is the hard way. It is two:
Who is on the receiving end — me, you, or something else?
How many, and if it is a thing, which gender?
The second question only bites in the bottom two rows, because only there does a noun decide. Me, te, nos and os are settled by the conversation itself: you always know who is talking.
So the difficulty is not eight-eighths of this table. It is one quarter of it.

segments.prompt: Give all eight direct object pronouns.
acceptedResponses: me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las
me te lo la nos os los las

feedback.incorrect: me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las.

segments.prompt: Which four of the eight need you to know a noun's gender?

feedback.correct: One quarter of the grid carries all of the difficulty.
feedback.incorrect: lo, la, los and las. The rest are settled by who is speaking.

segments.prompt: Which two of the eight did you never have to be taught?

feedback.correct: You made them yourself with an -s.
feedback.incorrect: Los and las — the plural of lo and la, and nothing more.

segments.text: How many direct object pronouns are there? (Eight.) How many of them depend on a noun? (Four.) Next: what all eight are for, in a conversation that would be unbearable without them.
